His point for that example was that the necessary tools to attack the problem hadn't yet been developed so it was a fruitless endeavor. While many very important problems are tractable. comments.text_zh: Don Eyles 关于为登月舱编程的写作（那正是他亲手做过的事！）非常精彩 [1]。那个网站上还有一个照片画廊，而且他还写了一整本书！另外，在 Bret Victor 的参考文献页面 [2] 上到处点点看——那真是座宝库。尽管我总担心一提它就会让它消失，但东西得分享出去才有用。那是一大批经典论文和访谈的合集。有人提到了《As You May Think》，它就在那里，Bush 约二十年后写的那篇后续也在，还有 Douglas Engelbart 本人那份带部分批注的原文版本！也去看看 folklore [3]，那是一堆关于苹果早期工作经历的好故事，出自在那里工作过的人之手（我相当确定主要是 Andy Hertzfeld）。最后，去找找 John Drury Clark 的《Ignition!》[4]，这有点跑题，但非常惊艳——它讲的是火箭发动机设计史，主要是其中那些疯狂的实验和化学，而且写得非常好。我不太想直接链一个 pdf 过去，不过要找也不难。附带说一句，这个不算那么历史性，但这是一篇很棒的励志文章：Richard Hamming 的《You and Your Research》（文字稿 [5]，视频版 [6]）。它谈到在 Bell Labs 工作的经历，以及那里不同人之间不同的文化元素，借此分析是什么让某些人真正卓越。1 - [LINK] 2 - [LINK] 3 - [LINK] 4 - [LINK] 5 - [LINK] 6 - [VIDEO]
comments.text: Don Eyles' writing about programming the lunar module (which was something he did!) is fantastic [1]. There's also a gallery of photos on that site and he has a whole book! And, click around on Bret Victor's references page[2] -- it's a real treasure. Despite my constant fear that mentioning it will make it go away, it needs to be shared to be useful. It's a big collection of classic papers and interviews. Someone mentioned "As You May Think", which is on there, as is Bush's follow-up from ~20 years later, and Douglas Engelbart's own partly annotated version of the original! Also check out folklore[3], which is a great bunch of stories about working at Apple in its early days, by people who worked there (mostly Andy Hertzfeld, I'm pretty sure). Lastly, look up "Ignition!" by John Drury Clark[4], which is a tangent, but is amazing -- it's about the history of the design of rocket engines, largely about the wild experiments and chemical science involved, and is very well written. I didn't feel right finding a pdf to link straight to, but they aren't that hard to find. As a bonus, this isn't so much historical, but it's a great inspirational essay, Richard Hamming's "You and Your Research"(transcript[5], a video version[6]). Talks about working at Bell Labs and the different cultural elements there across people as part of analysing what makes certain people truly great. 1 - [LINK] 2 - [LINK] 3 - [LINK] 4 - [LINK] 5 - [LINK] 6 - [VIDEO]

comments.author: nicklaf
comments.story_title: The fertility of the older mind
comments.why_zh: Hamming 建议研究成功而非失败
comments.quote_zh: 研究成功。如果你研究成功，当时机来临时，你就会知道如何成功。
comments.text_zh: 确实，我们应该能坦然地进行尝试，不必担心出丑，也要学会偶尔容忍更严重的失败；而且意外的失败确实能让人注意到更深层问题的征兆——这些问题值得在它们日后给你带来更大麻烦之前加以纠正。不过，我要指出 Richard Hamming 的建议：要从成功中学习，而不是从失败中学习。“出错的方式有那么多，正确的方式却那么少，所以研究成功要经济得多。”还有：“研究成功。如果你研究成功，当时机来临时，你就会知道如何成功。如果你研究失败，那你就只会知道如何失败。所以要非常仔细地研究成功：不只是你自己的，还有别人的。伽利略为什么做了他所做的事？牛顿是怎么做到的？尽你所能去研究别人：他们如何成功，他们成功的要素是什么，其中哪些要素你能融入自己的个性。你不可能成为所有人，但你必须找到自己的方法。研究成功是塑造你自己风格的一个非常好的途径。”（后一段引文出自 [VIDEO] 的 25:30 处）
comments.text: It's true that we ought to be comfortable experimenting without fear of embarrassment, as well as to learn to tolerate more serious failure on occasion, and certainly unexpected failures can serve to draw attention to symptoms of deeper issues worthy of rectifying before they cause you even greater trouble down the road. However, I will point to Richard Hamming's advice to learn from our successes rather than our failures. "There are so many ways of being wrong and so few ways of being right that it is much more economical to study successes." And: "Study successes. If you study successes, when your time comes, you'll know how to succeed. If you study failures, then you'll know how to fail. So study success very closely: not only yours, but other people's. Why did Galileo do what he did? How did Newton do it? Try as best you can to study other people: how they succeed, and what the elements of their success are, which elements of that can you adapt to your personality. You can't be everybody, but you have to find your own method. Studying success is a very good way of informing your own style." (The latter quote is from 25:30 of [VIDEO] )

comments.why_zh: Hamming 谈知识如何像复利一样随努力积累
comments.quote_zh: 知识和生产力就像复利。
comments.text_zh:
考虑到提到了 Bell Labs，你可能想到的是 Hamming 的演讲 “You and Your Research”（[LINK]），其中提到了那个想法：

> 现在说说动力的问题。你会注意到，大多数伟大的科学家都有极强的动力。我在 Bell Labs 和 John Tukey 共事了十年。他的动力极强。有一天，大约是我加入后的三四年，我发现 John Tukey 其实比我稍微年轻一点。John 是个天才，而我显然不是。于是我冲进 Bode 的办公室说：“我这个年纪的人怎么可能知道得像 John Tukey 那么多？”他往椅背上一靠，双手枕在脑后，微微一笑，说：“Hamming，你会惊讶的，如果你像他那样努力那么多年，你会知道多少。”我只好灰溜溜地溜出了办公室！

> Bode 的意思是：“知识和生产力就像复利。”假设两个人能力大致相当，其中一个人比另一个人多付出百分之十的努力，后者的产出会超过前者的两倍。你知道得越多，就学得越多；学得越多，你能做的就越多；你能做的越多，机会就越多——这非常像复利。我不想给你一个具体利率，但它是非常高的利率。假设两个人能力完全相同，那个日复一日设法多挤出一小时思考的人，一生中的生产力会高得多。

在已发布版本中略有编辑
comments.text: Given the Bell Labs mention, you may be thinking of Hamming's talk “You and Your Research” ( [LINK] ), where that idea is mentioned: > Now for the matter of drive. You observe that most great scientists have tremendous drive. I worked for ten years with John Tukey at Bell Labs. He had tremendous drive. One day about three or four years after I joined, I discovered that John Tukey was slightly younger than I was. John was a genius and I clearly was not. Well I went storming into Bode's office and said, “How can anybody my age know as much as John Tukey does?” He leaned back in his chair, put his hands behind his head, grinned slightly, and said, “You would be surprised Hamming, how much you would know if you worked as hard as he did that many years.” I simply slunk out of the office! > What Bode was saying was this: “Knowledge and productivity are like compound interest.” Given two people of approximately the same ability and one person who works ten percent more than the other, the latter will more than twice outproduce the former. The more you know, the more you learn; the more you learn, the more you can do; the more you can do, the more the opportunity - it is very much like compound interest. I don't want to give you a rate, but it is a very high rate. Given two people with exactly the same ability, the one person who manages day in and day out to get in one more hour of thinking will be tremendously more productive over a lifetime. Slightly edited in the version publishe
